The class of a halogen derivative is decided by the kind of carbon the halogen is joined to.

The vinylic halide is **(B)** \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-X}\), in which the halogen is attached **directly** to a doubly bonded \(sp^2\) carbon.

The other three are:

- \(\mathrm{R-CH(X)-R}\) - the halogen is on an \(sp^3\) carbon of a saturated chain, so this is a **secondary alkyl halide**.
- \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-X}\) - the halogen is joined to the benzene ring itself, so this is an **aryl halide**.
- \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-CH_2-X}\) - the halogen is on the \(sp^3\) carbon **next to** a doubly bonded carbon, so this is an **allylic halide**.

**Step 1.** At 423-600 K ethane and nitric acid react in the vapour phase. A hydrogen of the alkane is replaced by the nitro group and the elements of water are removed.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_3} + \mathrm{HNO_3} \xrightarrow{\text{423-600 K}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

**A is nitroethane**, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NO_2}\).

**Step 2.** Tin with concentrated hydrochloric acid supplies nascent hydrogen, which reduces the nitro group to an amino group.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NO_2} + 6[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow[\text{conc. HCl}]{\mathrm{Sn}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}\)

**B is ethylamine**, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\).

The same nitroethane can be obtained from a halogen derivative by warming ethyl bromide with silver nitrite, and from either route it is reduced to ethylamine in the same way.

**(B)** \(2,3\text{-dimethylbutane}\)

**Step 1.** 1-Chloropropane with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) undergoes dehydrohalogenation: the hydroxide ion acts as a base, removes a \(\beta\)-hydrogen, and the chlorine leaves from the adjacent carbon.

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc. KOH}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2} + \mathrm{KCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

**B is propene.**

**Step 2.** No peroxide is present, so \(\mathrm{HBr}\) adds by Markownikoff's rule: the hydrogen goes to the carbon already carrying more hydrogens and the bromine to the middle carbon.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2} + \mathrm{HBr} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_3}\)

**C is 2-bromopropane.**

**Step 3.** Sodium in dry ether couples two molecules of the halide - the Wurtz reaction - joining the two carbons that carried the bromine.

\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_3} + 2\,\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH(CH_3)_2} + 2\,\mathrm{NaBr}\)

**D is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH(CH_3)_2}\), 2,3-dimethylbutane.**

Had a peroxide been present in step 2 the addition would have been anti-Markownikoff, C would have been 1-bromopropane, and the Wurtz product would have been the straight chain hexane; it is the absence of peroxide that fixes the answer at the branched alkane.

**(i) Alcoholic solution of potassium hydroxide.** In alcohol the hydroxide ion acts as a **base**: it removes a \(\beta\)-hydrogen while the halogen leaves from the adjacent carbon, so an alkene is formed by dehydrohalogenation.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2Br} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc. KOH}} \mathrm{CH_2=CH_2} + \mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is **ethene**.

**(ii) Moist silver oxide.** Moist silver oxide is \(\mathrm{Ag_2O}\) with water, which supplies the hydroxide ion. Here the hydroxide acts as a **nucleophile**, attacks the carbon and displaces bromide, which is removed as insoluble silver bromide.

\(2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{Ag_2O} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + 2\,\mathrm{AgBr} \downarrow\)

The product is **ethanol**.

**(iii) Silver acetate.** The acetate ion is the nucleophile; it displaces bromide from the carbon and an ester is formed.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{CH_3COOAg} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5} + \mathrm{AgBr} \downarrow\)

The product is **ethyl acetate** (ethyl ethanoate).

**(i) Ethyl bromide to ethyl methyl ether.** Sodium methoxide supplies the methoxide ion, which acts as the nucleophile and displaces bromide. This is **Williamson's ether synthesis**.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{CH_3ONa} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5-O-CH_3} + \mathrm{NaBr}\)

**(ii) Ethyl bromide to ethene.** Alcoholic potassium hydroxide brings about dehydrohalogenation.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2Br} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc. KOH}} \mathrm{CH_2=CH_2} + \mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

**(iii) Bromobenzene to toluene.** An aryl halide and an alkyl halide are coupled by sodium in dry ether. This is the **Wurtz-Fittig reaction**.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-Br} + \mathrm{CH_3Br} + 2\,\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_3} + 2\,\mathrm{NaBr}\)

**(iv) Chlorobenzene to biphenyl.** Only the aryl halide takes part, so the coupling is called the **Fittig reaction**.

\(2\,\mathrm{C_6H_5-Cl} + 2\,\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-C_6H_5} + 2\,\mathrm{NaCl}\)

Silver acetate supplies the **acetate ion**, which acts as the nucleophile and displaces bromide from the carbon; the silver ion assists by taking the bromide out of the reaction as insoluble silver bromide. An ester is formed.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{CH_3COOAg} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5} + \mathrm{AgBr} \downarrow\)

The product is **ethyl acetate** (ethyl ethanoate), \(\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5}\).

**Dehydrohalogenation of 2-chlorobutane.** When 2-chlorobutane is heated with a concentrated **alcoholic** solution of potassium hydroxide, the hydroxide ion acts as a **base**. It removes a hydrogen from a carbon next to the one carrying the halogen (a \(\beta\)-hydrogen), while the chlorine leaves as chloride ion from the \(\alpha\)-carbon. The two groups eliminated come from adjacent carbons, so this is a \(\beta\)-elimination, and a carbon-carbon double bond is formed.

2-Chlorobutane carries \(\beta\)-hydrogens on **two different** carbons, so two alkenes are possible.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CHCl-CH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc. KOH}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH=CH_2}\)

By **Saytzeff's rule** the alkene carrying the greater number of alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons is the more stable and predominates. So **but-2-ene is the major product** and but-1-ene the minor one.

**Uses of CFC.** Chlorofluorocarbons, the freons, for example \(\mathrm{CCl_2F_2}\) (freon-12), are volatile, non-toxic, non-flammable and chemically unreactive. They are therefore used as **refrigerants** in refrigerators and air conditioners, as **propellants** in aerosol sprays, as **blowing agents** for plastic foams, and as solvents for cleaning electronic components.

**Environmental effect of CFC.** That same unreactivity is the problem: a CFC molecule is not destroyed in the lower atmosphere and slowly diffuses up into the stratosphere. There ultraviolet radiation breaks a carbon-chlorine bond and sets free a chlorine radical, which attacks ozone.

\(\mathrm{CCl_2F_2} \xrightarrow{\text{UV}} \mathrm{CClF_2}^{\bullet} + \mathrm{Cl}^{\bullet}\)

\(\mathrm{Cl}^{\bullet} + \mathrm{O_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{ClO}^{\bullet} + \mathrm{O_2}\)

\(\mathrm{ClO}^{\bullet} + \mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cl}^{\bullet} + \mathrm{O_2}\)

The chlorine radical is regenerated in the second step, so one radical destroys ozone molecule after ozone molecule. The ozone layer is depleted, more ultraviolet radiation reaches the earth, and the risk of skin cancer, cataract and damage to crops rises.

Silver cyanide in alcohol is the reagent. The cyanide ion is **ambident** - it can attack through its carbon or through its nitrogen. In the silver salt the cyanide is largely covalent, so the free carbon end is not available and the **nitrogen** attacks the carbon of the alkyl halide; an **isocyanide** is formed. Potassium cyanide, being ionic, would give the cyanide (nitrile) instead, because there the carbon attacks.

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{AgCN} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc.}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-N} \!\equiv\! \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{AgCl} \downarrow\)

The product is **ethyl isocyanide** (ethyl carbylamine), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NC}\).

**(b) Ethyl cyanide from ethyl bromide.**

Ethyl bromide is heated with an **alcoholic solution of potassium cyanide**. Potassium cyanide is ionic, so the cyanide ion is free and attacks through its **carbon**; the bromide is displaced and a **nitrile** is formed.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{KCN} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc.}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-C} \!\equiv\! \mathrm{N} + \mathrm{KBr}\)

The product is **ethyl cyanide**, that is **propanenitrile**, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5CN}\). Note that the new molecule has three carbons: the two of the ethyl group and the one gained from the cyanide.

Silver cyanide in place of potassium cyanide would give ethyl isocyanide instead, because the silver salt lets the nitrogen attack.

**(a) Silver nitrite.** The nitrite ion is **ambident**. With the silver salt the **nitrogen** attacks the carbon, so a **nitroalkane** is obtained; sodium nitrite would give the alkyl nitrite instead, because there the oxygen attacks.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{AgNO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5-NO_2} + \mathrm{AgBr} \downarrow\)

The product is **nitroethane**.

**(b) Magnesium in dry ether.** Magnesium inserts itself into the carbon-halogen bond and a **Grignard reagent** is formed. The ether must be dry, since even traces of water would decompose the reagent to ethane.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{Mg} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_2H_5MgBr}\)

The product is **ethylmagnesium bromide**.

**(c) Alcoholic sodium hydroxide.** In alcohol the hydroxide ion acts as a base, removes a \(\beta\)-hydrogen, and the halogen leaves from the adjacent carbon, so dehydrohalogenation takes place.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2Br} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc. NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_2=CH_2} + \mathrm{NaBr} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is **ethene**.

**(i) Bromobenzene.** An aryl halide and an alkyl halide are coupled by **sodium metal in dry ether**; this is the **Wurtz-Fittig reaction**, and the equation is written below with that reagent.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-Br} + \mathrm{CH_3Br} + 2\,\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_3} + 2\,\mathrm{NaBr}\)

The product is **toluene** (methylbenzene).

**(ii) Mercurous fluoride.** Heating an alkyl bromide with a metallic fluoride exchanges the halogen for fluorine. This halogen exchange is the **Swartz reaction**, and it is the practical way of making an alkyl fluoride, since direct fluorination of an alkane is too violent to control.

\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3Br} + \mathrm{Hg_2F_2} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CH_3F} + \mathrm{Hg_2Br_2}\)

The product is **fluoromethane** (methyl fluoride).

Sodium metal in dry ether couples two molecules of the aryl halide. When only an aryl halide takes part, the coupling is called the **Fittig reaction**.

\(2\,\mathrm{C_6H_5-Cl} + 2\,\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-C_6H_5} + 2\,\mathrm{NaCl}\)

Structure of the product: two benzene rings joined **directly** to each other by a single carbon-carbon bond, one hydrogen having been removed from each ring position that carried the chlorine.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-C_6H_5}\)

The product is **biphenyl**.

Fuming sulphuric acid (oleum) supplies the electrophile \(\mathrm{SO_3}\), so chlorobenzene undergoes **electrophilic substitution on the ring** - sulphonation.

The chlorine withdraws electrons from the ring through the sigma bond, but it also donates a lone pair into the ring by resonance. The resonance effect places the extra electron density at the positions **ortho and para** to the chlorine, and the electrophile enters there.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-Cl} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \xrightarrow{\text{fuming}} \mathrm{Cl-C_6H_4-SO_3H} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Both the ortho and the para product are formed. The **para** isomer, **4-chlorobenzenesulphonic acid**, is the major product, because the position opposite the chlorine is free of the steric crowding that hinders attack next to it.

**(C)** Swarts reaction

An alkyl chloride or bromide heated with a **metallic fluoride** - silver fluoride, mercurous fluoride, antimony trifluoride or cobalt fluoride - exchanges its halogen for fluorine.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{AgF} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2F} + \mathrm{AgCl}\)

This halogen exchange with a metallic fluoride is the **Swartz reaction**. It is the practical route to an alkyl fluoride, because direct fluorination of an alkane is far too violent to control.

The other three named reactions do something else. The **Finkelstein** reaction is the corresponding exchange for **iodine**, an alkyl chloride or bromide being heated with sodium iodide in dry acetone. **Williamson's** synthesis makes an **ether** from an alkyl halide and a sodium alkoxide. The **Wurtz** reaction couples two molecules of an alkyl halide with sodium in dry ether to give an **alkane**.

| Point of difference | \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism | \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Number of steps | Two: slow heterolysis of the C-X bond, then fast attack by the nucleophile | One only; the bond to the nucleophile forms as the bond to the halogen breaks |
| Intermediate or transition state | A planar **carbocation** intermediate is formed | No intermediate; a **pentacoordinate transition state** is formed |
| Rate law | rate \(= k\,[\text{halide}]\), first order | rate \(= k\,[\text{halide}][\text{nucleophile}]\), second order |
| Molecularity of the slow step | Unimolecular | Bimolecular |
| Effect of the nucleophile | The rate does not depend on its concentration or its strength, since it is absent from the slow step | The rate rises with both its concentration and its strength |
| Stereochemistry at a chiral carbon | Largely **racemisation**, since the planar carbocation can be attacked from either face | **Inversion** of configuration (Walden inversion), since attack is from the side opposite the halogen |
| Order of reactivity of the halide | \(3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > \mathrm{CH_3X}\), following carbocation stability | \(\mathrm{CH_3X} > 1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ\), following freedom from crowding at the carbon |
| Solvent that favours it | Polar protic, which solvates and stabilises the carbocation | Polar aprotic, which leaves the nucleophile free to attack |
| Example | \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Br} + \mathrm{OH^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-OH} + \mathrm{Br^-}\) | \(\mathrm{CH_3-Br} + \mathrm{OH^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-OH} + \mathrm{Br^-}\) |

The two paths therefore differ above all in the slow step: in \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) the halide alone breaks apart in it, while in \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) the halide and the nucleophile meet in it.

**(B)** Swarts reaction

Methyl chloride is heated with a **metallic fluoride** - silver fluoride, mercurous fluoride, antimony trifluoride or cobalt fluoride - and the chlorine is exchanged for fluorine.

\(\mathrm{CH_3Cl} + \mathrm{AgF} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3F} + \mathrm{AgCl}\)

or, with mercurous fluoride,

\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3Cl} + \mathrm{Hg_2F_2} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CH_3F} + \mathrm{Hg_2Cl_2}\)

This exchange of halogen for fluorine using a metallic fluoride is the **Swartz reaction**, and it is how an alkyl fluoride is made in practice.

The other three are different reactions. The **Finkelstein** reaction exchanges chlorine or bromine for **iodine**, using sodium iodide in dry acetone. **Williamson's** synthesis makes an **ether** from an alkyl halide and a sodium alkoxide. The **Wurtz** reaction couples two alkyl halide molecules with sodium in dry ether to give an **alkane**.

**Density of silver.**

For a face centred cubic unit cell the number of particles per unit cell is \(n = 4\).

Given: \(a = 400\ \mathrm{pm} = 400 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm} = 4.00 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}\), \(M = 108\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\), \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).

\(\rho = \dfrac{n M}{a^{3} N_A}\)

\(a^{3} = (4.00 \times 10^{-8})^{3} = 6.4 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^{3}}\)

\(\rho = \dfrac{4 \times 108}{6.4 \times 10^{-23} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}} = \dfrac{432}{38.54}\)

\(\therefore \rho = 11.21\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}}\)

Silver is a heavy metal whose measured density is about \(10.5\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}}\), so a value of this size is what the data should give; the small excess follows from the rounded edge length of 400 pm, the true edge length being close to 409 pm.

**Note on the haloform reaction.**

Ethanol, or any alcohol of the type \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-R}\), or a methyl ketone \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-R}\), when warmed with a halogen \(\mathrm{(Cl_2}\), \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) or \(\mathrm{I_2)}\) and an alkali gives a **haloform**, \(\mathrm{CHX_3}\).

The three hydrogens of the methyl group next to the carbonyl carbon are replaced one after another by halogen, and the alkali then cleaves the resulting trihalomethyl group from the rest of the molecule. With iodine and sodium hydroxide, ethanol gives iodoform:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + 4\,\mathrm{I_2} + 6\,\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CHI_3} \downarrow + \mathrm{HCOONa} + 5\,\mathrm{NaI} + 5\,\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Iodoform separates as a **yellow crystalline solid** with a characteristic smell, so this reaction serves as a test for ethanol, for the \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-}\) grouping and for a methyl ketone. The same reaction with bleaching powder gives chloroform, and with bromine and alkali gives bromoform; all three products are polyhalogen compounds.

answer:
The salient features of the \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) mechanism are:

1. **It is a single step reaction.** The bond to the nucleophile is formed at the same moment as the bond to the halogen is broken, so no intermediate is ever obtained.

2. **The nucleophile attacks from the back.** It approaches the carbon from the side **opposite** the halogen, along the line of the carbon-halogen bond, because the halogen side of the molecule is both crowded and rich in electrons.

3. **A pentacoordinate transition state is formed.** At the top of the energy barrier the carbon is joined to five groups: the incoming nucleophile and the departing halogen are each partly bonded and lie in a straight line through the carbon, while the three remaining groups lie in a plane passing through it.

4. **The kinetics are of second order.** Both the halide and the nucleophile take part in the only step, so

\(\text{rate} = k\,[\mathrm{R-X}][\mathrm{Nu^-}]\)

and the reaction is bimolecular.

5. **The configuration is inverted.** As the nucleophile pushes in from the back, the other three groups are turned through the plane of the carbon like an umbrella turning inside out. A chiral carbon therefore emerges with its configuration **inverted**, which is called Walden inversion.

6. **The order of reactivity is** \(\mathrm{CH_3X} > 1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ\). Every extra alkyl group on the carbon crowds it and blocks the backside approach, so a tertiary halide hardly reacts by this path.

7. **It is favoured by** a strong nucleophile in high concentration and a polar aprotic solvent, which does not surround the nucleophile and hold it back.

\(\mathrm{HO^-} + \mathrm{CH_3-Br} \longrightarrow [\mathrm{HO} \cdots \mathrm{CH_3} \cdots \mathrm{Br}]^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-OH} + \mathrm{Br^-}\)
